---
title: "Predictive modeling of claims status"
author: 'Alison Gu, Jocelyn Lee, Clark Enge, Elijah Gabriel Ret, Nic Chan'
date: today
---

### Abstract

We trained our models on 2,165 labeled webpages and used them to classify 929 unlabeled test pages. Text was taken from each page's title, meta description, headers and paragraphs, and represented as TF-IDF scores for words and two-word phrases (bigrams). For binary classification we used a linear support vector machine (SVM), which reached 84.3% accuracy in 5-fold cross-validation. For multiclass classification we paired that binary SVM with a second linear SVM trained only on relevant pages, which reached 83.4% accuracy.

### Preprocessing

We parsed every raw page, including pages missing standard HTML tags, so that no page was dropped and all 929 test pages receive a prediction. After removing `<script>` and `<style>` content, we extracted two groups of text: page metadata (title and meta descriptions) and main content (headers and paragraphs). Text was cleaned by removing links, emails, numbers and punctuation, splitting camelCase words and lowercasing. We then tokenized into words, dropped stopwords, stemmed each word to its root and added adjacent-word bigrams. Terms appearing in at least 3 pages and at most 95% of pages were kept, giving a vocabulary of about 31,600 terms. Each page became a row of L2-normalized TF-IDF scores, with metadata terms kept as separate features from content terms.

### Methods

**Binary.** A linear SVM (e1071, cost = 1) with Platt-scaled probabilities predicts whether a page has relevant claim content. Pages with predicted probability above 0.5 are labeled relevant, and all others are labeled `N/A`. Accuracy was estimated with stratified 5-fold cross-validation, refitting the TF-IDF vocabulary inside each fold to avoid leakage. The final model was then trained on all 2,165 labeled pages.

**Multiclass.** We used a two-step design so that the binary and multiclass predictions always agree. Pages the binary SVM labels `N/A` also get `N/A` as their multiclass label. Pages labeled relevant are passed to a second linear SVM (cost = 1), trained only on relevant pages, which assigns whichever of the four claim categories has the highest probability. This model was evaluated with the same 5-fold cross-validation and refit on all labeled pages.

### Results

All estimates come from 5-fold cross-validation on the 2,165 labeled pages (± one standard error across folds).

**Binary** (positive class = relevant claim content)

| Accuracy      | Sensitivity | Specificity |
|---------------|-------------|-------------|
| 0.843 ± 0.013 | 0.855       | 0.830       |

**Multiclass** (overall accuracy 0.834 ± 0.013; per-class values are one-vs-rest)

| Class                         | Sensitivity | Specificity |
|-------------------------------|-------------|-------------|
| N/A: No relevant content      | 0.830       | 0.855       |
| Physical Activity             | 0.746       | 0.976       |
| Possible Fatality             | 0.921       | 0.964       |
| Potentially unlawful activity | 0.898       | 0.975       |
| Other claim content           | 0.465       | 0.980       |
| **Macro average**             | **0.772**   | **0.950**   |

Most multiclass errors come from confusing relevant pages with `N/A`, not from confusing one claim category with another. The exception is "Other claim content", the smallest and least specific class, which is often predicted as `N/A`.
